title: Do Students Even Want AI?
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Marcinek argues that schools keep repeating the same ed-tech cycle of excitement, rapid adoption, exhaustion and reflection, and that AI is the latest turn of it. Drawing on a 1:1 iPad rollout he led, where many students barely switched the devices on, he shows that the failure was one of listening rather than technology. His central question, whether students even want AI in their learning, reframes adoption as a dialogue with students rather than a directive. He distinguishes reactivity from responsiveness and says responsiveness can mean attunement rather than speed. He closes with a concrete alternative to another AI in Education session, a professional development day built on teacher and student panels and a co-designed tech values statement. The tone is reflective and school-policy focused rather than a product evaluation.
points: Ed-tech waves fail when plans are built around tools rather than people, and the first question, why, and what students think of it, is routinely skipped.
Responsiveness is not speed; it means observing classrooms and gathering student stories before implementing, rather than reacting to external pressure.
Relationships sustain learning even when technology assists it, so any AI adoption should be tested against whether it deepens or replaces human connection.
A practical PD design is teacher and student panels, small-group discussion of where technology helps or distracts, and a co-written tech values statement.
quotes: Each time, the pattern repeats: a rush of excitement, followed by rapid adoption, and then the slow realization that we never stopped long enough to ask if we were solving the right problem. The technology may change, but the rhythm remains the same — enthusiasm, implementation, exhaustion, reflection — and then the next new thing arrives.
It wasn’t a failure of technology. It was a failure of listening. We built a plan around tools, not around people.

Ask someone how they arrived at their career or passion, and they won’t say “an iPad.” They’ll name a teacher — someone who inspired, challenged, or believed in them. Technology may assist learning, but relationships sustain it.

The EdTech cycle repeats because we too often confuse reactivity with responsiveness. We rush to adopt before we reflect, to announce before we assess, to implement before we listen. Breaking this pattern means slowing down — not to resist innovation, but to make it meaningful.

To be both responsive and thoughtful is to accept that progress and patience can coexist. Responsiveness doesn’t have to mean speed — it can mean attunement. It’s the willingness to observe what’s happening in classrooms, to gather stories from students, and to let those insights shape our next steps.

Sometimes the most forward-thinking move isn’t chasing the next shiny thing — it’s polishing what’s already in our hands. Before we rush to roll out the next new technology, perhaps the real work is to pause and look inward.
